articles.title: NATO warns Russia: 'We will break' forces, destroy 'anything and everything' if you attack
articles.summary: Gen. Alexus Grynkewich outlined NATO's strategy to "block, blunt and break" enemy forces at the Warsaw Security Forum amid rising Russia tensions.
articles.body: NATO's top military commander warned Monday that what he called the "lethal alliance" would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault. "Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us," U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, in an apparent warning to Moscow. "This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force," he said during a panel titled "Theory of Victory: How Do We Achieve Military Success Against Russia in Deterrence and Defence?" on the first day of the forum. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS Grynkewich, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe, also outlined a three-pronged strategy of "blocking, blunting and breaking" enemy forces, making clear that while NATO is a defensive alliance, it is prepared to respond decisively to an assault on any of its 32 members. "If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile." The warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow. "We stand here together in Poland today stronger than ever united in our common vision of a more balanced, more ready and more lethal alliance," Grynkewich also said. European officials have accused Russia of waging a campaign of hybrid warfare involving sabotage, arson and cyberattacks, alongside increasingly provocative military activity near NATO territory. I’M PRESIDENT OF ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST RELIABLE ALLIES. HERE’S HOW WE STAND UP TO RUSSIA In 2025, multiple Russian drones entered Polish airspace during a large-scale attack on Ukraine, prompting a response from Polish and allied aircraft. NATO launched Operation Eastern Sentry to strengthen defenses along its eastern flank. Romania has also reported Russian drone incursions, while Estonia has accused Russian military aircraft of violating its airspace. Grynkewich's remarks had followed a tense weekend between Russia and Ukraine, with Moscow launching fresh strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite diplomatic efforts to reduce hostilities. President Donald Trump had announced that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the U.S. and global markets. ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE The reported agreement included a waiver of certain U.S. sanctions on Russian energy exports. Zelenskyy went on to accuse Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities, casting doubt on prospects for a broader ceasefire. The tensions have also been accompanied by recent nuclear warnings from Moscow. On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania. In a diplomatic note obtained by Reuters, Moscow accused NATO of pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" that carried "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict." According to the note, Russia warned it could use its full military arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend Kaliningrad and raised the possibility of strikes against decision-making centers in NATO countries at the outset of a conflict. RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte rejected the threats, emphasizing the alliance's defensive mission and calling on Moscow to end its war in Ukraine. "Putin knows that he can never win from NATO," Rutte said during a Sept. 30 appearance at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit. Putin has also maintained that Russia has no plans to attack European countries and wants peaceful coexistence with its neighbors. Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name during his Warsaw address, but his warning appeared directed at Moscow and with NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept also identifying Russia as the most significant and direct threat to allied security. "My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance," Grynkewich said on Monday. "And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us." Grynkewich said NATO was already putting the strategy into action through military exercises, enhanced military readiness and investments in new capabilities. SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE. NOW EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS "If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent," he said. The general made clear that NATO's response would not necessarily be limited to enemy troops directly involved in an assault, but could extend to the broader military infrastructure enabling the attack. Meanwhile, Trump has pressed European allies to increase defense spending and has questioned whether countries that fail to meet their obligations should expect U.S. protection. Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington's commitment, recalling Trump's positive remarks about the alliance during the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, Netherlands. "I was in the room and I felt the love," Grynkewich said of the 2025 event. "What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we've got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it," he added. He also indicated a willingness to discuss suspected hybrid attacks more openly if individual NATO governments wanted him to address their concerns. "If a nation wants me to, I'm happy to talk about it," he said. articles.title: Houston man run over by ICE vehicle will need additional surgery, advocates say
articles.summary: ICE has said he wasn’t the target of the attempted traffic stop. His team said he fled because the vehicle was unmarked and didn’t use sirens.
articles.body: HOUSTON — A man who was injured when an ICE officer’s car ran over him has had surgery on his leg but needs additional procedures to reconstruct the leg and other parts of his body, an advocate for the man said Monday. Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, had leg and hip injuries and a shattered ankle after the officer’s vehicle struck him during a pursuit Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, a co-founder and the executive director of FIEL, who was speaking on Parra’s behalf. Parra cannot put weight on his leg for six weeks and must wait for swelling to reduce before doctors can perform additional surgery, he said at a news conference Monday. Espinosa said Parra — who had gotten out of a vehicle and was on foot — was hit “in a violent and brutal fashion.” ICE has said it attempted a vehicle stop and the people in the car ran away. The officers tried to apprehend the fleeing men, and “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck,” it said. It has said Parra was not the target of the attempted stop. Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows. Video obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. The video shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running. It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in the shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows. The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not respond to a request for further comment. Parra was at a Houston area hospital Monday morning when his attorney and Espinosa visited him, Espinosa said. But they had only 10 or 15 minutes before ICE officers came in and began recording their conversation and forced them out, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said. “To add insult to injury, Mr. Miguel is in the custody of the ICE agents who ran him down,” Espinosa said. “This is so disheartening and so angering that Miguel has to face the people that brutally attacked them every single day, 24 hours a day.” Parra has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and he has no criminal record, Bruno told NBC News. DHS said he was in the country without legal permission. Bruno said he has never had encounters with immigration authorities. He and the man with him in the car do stucco work, she said. Neither Parra nor the other man in the car was the target of ICE in Saturday’s traffic stop, Bruno and Espinosa said. ICE identified the man it was targeting as Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who it said is not legally in the country and had been removed twice and entered the U.S. illegally five times. It said that Mendoza Cervantes had been arrested multiple times for drunken driving and once for unlawful possession of a firearm and that he had an active removal order. Bruno and Espinosa countered that neither Parra nor the man in the car with him, whom he had picked up for work, knew Mendoza Cervantes. The Civil Rights Division of the Harris County District Attorney’s Office sent investigators to the intersection where Parra was hit, said Damali Keith, a spokesman for the district attorney’s office. The Harris County Sheriff’s Office has said it is leading the investigation of what it described Saturday as an “auto-ped” incident, with help from the Harris County District Attorney’s Office. Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops. The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

articles.title: Why the Prime Minister wants to talk about Brexit again
articles.summary: For the first time since the UK left the EU, we have a prime minister who will "unflinchingly" debate Brexit, says the BBC's political editor Chris Mason.
articles.body:
For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.

I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017."

Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016.

And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020.

Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon.

With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street.

He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.

Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case.

First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement.

Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.

In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit.

"This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.

Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago.

"They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost , a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.

The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.

Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.

He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.

And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.

"I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.

In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.

His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt – calling the prime minister "a liar."

The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

And so a debate resumes about the difference between attempted interference, interference and successful interference.

But the key point is this: for the first time since the UK left the European Union, we now have a prime minister who is willing to unflinchingly debate Brexit: whether it is working, how it is working, how to improve it, and if it's proved to be a failure.

In so doing he hopes he can tap into public sentiment. Opinion polls suggest a perception among a majority that leaving the European Union has not turned out how many might have hoped.

On top of this, he hopes to lure pro Europeans broadly on the Left who may recently have supported the Liberal Democrats, the Green parties of both England and Wales and Scotland, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru towards Labour. That is the political logic from the government's point of view, for now at least.

And as for where all of this leads – well, good question. In the coming weeks, months and perhaps years, there may be a Back to the Future vibe to our political debate. A splash of familiarity, as a conversation about the relationship we have with our nearest neighbours resumes.

articles.title: A Jordanian princess recognised her custom-made engagement ring on an auction catalogue cover, leading to a court case over jewellery allegedly stolen from her London residence
articles.summary: An engagement ring made specially for a Jordanian princess became the starting point of a criminal investigation after it appeared in a British auction
articles.body: An engagement ring made specially for a Jordanian princess became the starting point of a criminal investigation after it appeared in a British auction catalogue in 2020. Princess Firyal Irshaid, now 81, told a London court that she had not authorised the sale of the ring or other pieces from her jewellery collection, which had remained at her Belgravia home while she was abroad during the Covid-19 pandemic. What began with a telephone call from a friend in the jewellery trade led her to examine catalogues from several earlier auctions and gather records to establish ownership. Her former housekeeper, Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, denies stealing jewellery from the property.Princess Firyal found her missing engagement ring on a UK auction catalogueThe discovery came in November 2020, when Pierre Jeannet, a friend of the princess and a partner at the high-end jewellery house JAR, contacted her about a piece he recognised. The ring had been created specifically for her engagement and was being used to feature the contents of an auction catalogue, the court heard.As reported by The Independent, Jeannet called Princess Firyal on 21 November to ask whether she was selling her jewellery. She said she was not. According to her evidence at Southwark Crown Court, he then explained that her engagement ring had appeared on the cover of a catalogue produced by Canterbury Auction Galleries.The ring was particularly identifiable because it had been made exclusively for her. The princess told jurors that no other example existed, making its appearance in the sale catalogue difficult to mistake for a similar piece.Once she realised what had happened, she began looking beyond that single item. Copies of catalogues covering sales held in March, May and August 2020 revealed further jewellery that she said belonged to her. She also contacted the auction house to challenge the sales, although she described its managing director, David Parker, as dismissive when she first explained her claim.Documents and photographs were used to establish ownershipPrincess Firyal said she had to assemble evidence from the records available to her in Jordan. The material included bills of sale, images reproduced in auction catalogues and photographs showing jewellery in her possession before it went missing.Among the photographs was one of the princess wearing a pair of earrings that she said had been stolen. Another showed a bracelet at her home. Such records became important in demonstrating that the items offered for sale were not simply pieces resembling jewellery in her collection, but objects she could identify as her own.The princess described collecting jewellery as a longstanding interest. She told the court that pieces were often left in open cupboards or on counters in her home, including items she had worn during the week. She said the collection was not kept under lock and key, leaving it accessible to people who entered the property.The princess left London at the start of the pandemicPrincess Firyal had travelled away from Britain in mid-March 2020, as the coronavirus pandemic was disrupting international travel. She told the court that her son telephoned her and gave her just three hours to pack and reach the airport.She recalled that the flight was the last one leaving before Jordan closed its airport. With no family around her in Britain, she said, she was determined to leave in time. Her Belgravia property was subsequently left with Taborda Henao, who had worked for her for 11 years.The housekeeper, 71, is accused of exploiting her access to the residence to steal the jewellery. The court heard that security guards assigned to the property were not permitted to enter the house and were required to remain outside while on duty.During the early stages of the pandemic, the princess also agreed to allow Taborda Henao's sister to stay at the property. The sister was later paid a salary, according to the evidence. Princess Firyal told jurors that she had initially found the arrangement unusual but accepted it. She was subsequently informed that the woman had become ill and left the house later that year.Police recovered jewellery during a search in FulhamThe investigation also involves Taborda Henao's nephew, Julian Ramirez, who prosecutors say played an important role in moving the allegedly stolen items towards their sale. According to the BBC, the court heard that £17,835 was transferred to the housekeeper by Ramirez between 23 June 2019 and 28 November 2020.Police later searched Taborda Henao's home in Fulham, where they found a wedding ring belonging to the princess, a pair of earrings and a necklace made from jewelled metal, according to the evidence presented at trial.Ramirez is believed to have travelled to Colombia in October 2023 while on police bail. Princess Firyal told the court that she had not known his name until police informed her that he was connected to the consignment of her jewellery to the auction house.You use AI every day. articles.title: Stolen Renoirs recovered in France thanks to DNA, vehicle tracking
articles.summary: One painting, “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano,” suffered a tear. The other, “Young Woman at the Well,” had slight damage to its frame, officials said.
articles.body: NANTERRE, France — DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday. Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said. One painting, “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano,” suffered a tear. The other, “Young Woman at the Well,” had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at $4.7 million. The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that “apparently caused the perpetrators to panic,” Bessone said. “As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve,” he said. Vehicle tracking led to the suspects The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said. Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said. Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection. The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003. Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent.” The paintings were hidden behind a wall The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of “theft committed by an organized gang” and “criminal association,” among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. They have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said. The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said. The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of “concealment” of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France. Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge. The theft renews concerns about museum security The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice. The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France. Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country “is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage” in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries. French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.

articles.title: Man admits to dismembering ex-girlfriend, keeping severed head in suitcase after she played him 'like a fool'
articles.summary: A New York man pleaded guilty to second-degree murder after he admitted that he murdered and dismembered his ex-girlfriend and kept her severed head in a suitcase.
articles.body: A New York man pleaded guilty to murdering and dismembering his ex-girlfriend and putting her severed head in a suitcase with a flower after she ended their relationship, later telling investigators she had "played me like a sucker," according to authorities. Damon Foy, 50, of Kerhonkson, pleaded guilty last week to second-degree murder in the 2024 death of Alberta Dale, 44, of Pennsylvania, according to the Ulster County District Attorney's Office. Between March 31 and April 1, 2024, Foy killed and dismembered Dale and was in the process of disposing of her body when law enforcement intervened, according to the district attorney's office. The Ulster County Sheriff's Office began investigating on April 1, 2024, after Dale's family members in Pennsylvania contacted law enforcement because they were concerned about her well-being, the district attorney's office said. Deputies first conducted a welfare check before launching a missing person investigation. SISTER OF MISSING DC MOM SPEAKS OUT AFTER EX’S ARREST EXPOSES 'HORRIFYING' ABUSIVE RELATIONSHIP Deputies first went to Foy’s apartment on April 1, 2024, and found Dale’s car, according to the New York Post. The next day, deputies returned to question Foy after a member of the public found Dale’s phone on the side of the road and turned it in to authorities, leading investigators to suspect potential foul play. "She’s in there," Foy whispered to investigators, when they arrived at his home during the missing person investigation. "I killed her," he added, according to court documents cited by the New York Post. Investigators obtained a search warrant for Foy's home and found a suitcase in a closet that contained the victim's remains. Foy was then arrested and charged in connection with Dale's death. After shining a flashlight on the suitcase, investigators "immediately noticed what appeared to be dried blood," according to the documents. "Officers opened the defendant’s suitcase and found Alberta Dale’s partial dismembered remains, including her severed head," the court documents read, according to the New York Post. "The remaining portions of her dismembered body were not located during the execution of the search warrant," the documents add. When he was later interviewed, Foy told investigators he "loved her," according to the documents. "The only thing she kept doing after the time throughout the whole relationship was just play me, play me like a fool, play me like a sucker, and just took advantage of the whole f–king system," he said. "That’s it. I was told to leave my own home. I was told to leave my own f–king home, not a bill in her name, and I was told to leave my own f–king home. Get out. Then it all started coming clearer to me," he added. When asked about the flower in the suitcase, Foy only said he was thinking about "what still happened last night to take s— over the top." Foy had a history of domestic violence against Dale, according to court documents cited by the New York Post. A previous domestic incident involved a gun, and investigators had also observed an axe at Foy’s property when they were searching for Dale. Dale had previously warned authorities that "if she went missing it was because [Foy] killed her," according to the court documents. Under a plea agreement, Foy is expected to receive 23 years to life behind bars, with a minimum term two years shorter than the maximum of 25 years to life, according to the Daily Freeman. MAN UNLEASHES DEADLY ‘REVENGE’ RAMPAGE ON EX’S FAMILY, KILLS 4 PEOPLE, 3 DOGS BEFORE TORCHING HOME: DA Chief Assistant District Attorney Liz Culmone-Mills told the outlet that the agreement was backed by Dale’s family. "The District Attorney’s Office would not be making this recommendation were it not for Alberta Dale’s family," Culmone-Mills told the outlet. Foy is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 16. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The total selfish disregard for the life and dignity of another person is at the heart of domestic violence; Damon Foy has shown that to us," District Attorney Emmanuel C. Nneji said in a statement. "We must recognize in our laws the rights of victims of domestic violence to be physically, psychologically, and emotionally safe from their tormentors and the dangers specifically targeted for them, and demand procedures that actually protect victims for real, not just on paper."

articles.title: Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack
articles.summary: Hackers raise temperatures in supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food in ‘large-scale’ cyberattack.
articles.body:
A cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France has raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.

Top retailers Intermarche, Cooperative U, E Leclerc and others confirmed the “unprecedented” cyberattack on Monday.

At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with more than 100 Cooperative U outlets, the retailers told the AFP news agency.

Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected, while Monoprix said about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit. E Leclerc said several of its stores were targeted.

The Paris prosecutor’s office said the “large-scale” ⁠attack had affected “connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France”. It led to food losses and fires, the office said.

The attack prompted Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to order France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office told the Reuters news agency.

The source said France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk.

There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”.

According to BFM TV, the hackers “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. The action resulted in the “destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products”, it said.

Intermarche told AFP that affected stores would have to “throw away all of the products” that were fresh or frozen.

Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Cooperative U, said the attack had disrupted refrigeration systems since Sunday night.

“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable,” he wrote on X.

He said the company’s teams were working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible, and that an investigation would be needed to “shed full light on this attack”.

Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control ⁠panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere.

The ⁠source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.

Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”.

The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, the company said, adding that it had “long advised customers” to keep their systems updated and replace older equipment.

The attack came after cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on August 9 describing vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems that could allow attackers to bypass authentication.

France’s retail federation, known as the FCD, called on Danfoss to provide “full transparency”.

It said some affected stores were already operating again.

Felix ⁠Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected.

Steven Lachance, a cybersecurity analyst, told Al Jazeera the attack was not unprecedented, though it was rare in its scale. He said that once a vulnerability is found in internet-connected equipment, cyber-attackers can log in remotely and trigger its features.

“We have connected infrastructure that is live on the internet, and that can be hacked. It’s a new reality,” he said, describing the attack as “a global wake-up call”.

“We absolutely need national and international measures to prevent these attacks, because otherwise it’s just going to keep happening,” he said.

While retailers had lost millions of euros in food, the next target could be worse, Lachance warned. “It could target energy infrastructure or hospitals,” he said.

articles.title: Kroger, one of America's oldest grocery chain to layoff thousands; largest in its 143-year history, here's what CEO told employees at townhall
articles.summary: America's oldest retail chain Kroger Co plans to eliminate roughly 3,000 corporate positions over the next three years, marking a sweeping workforce
articles.body: America's oldest retail chain Kroger Co plans to eliminate roughly 3,000 corporate positions over the next three years, marking a sweeping workforce reduction as new Chief Executive Officer Greg Foran moves to overhaul the grocer’s management structure. The cuts represent more than one-third of Kroger’s approximately 8,200 corporate staff, making the restructuring one of the largest corporate employees' reductions in the supermarket chain’s 143-year history.Foran, a former Walmart executive, who joined the retailer in February this year, detailed the turnaround strategy in a memo to employees following a companywide meeting on Monday, October 12. The restructuring comes as America's largest traditional grocer contends with slowing top-line growth, fierce retail competition, and persistent inflationary pressures impacting consumer spending. The memo outlined plans to eliminate redundant functions across departments while modernizing daily operations. Kroger is increasingly turning to emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, to automate workflows and drive efficiencies across its corporate network.What CEO Greg Foran told employees at townhallThe Cincinnati-based grocery giant announced the layoffs to its employees during an all-company call Monday, October 12. In the memo sent to Kroger employees obtained by the Business Courier, CEO Greg Foran wrote that the company’s transformation will result in the company reducing its corporate workforce across multiple functions by about 3,000 roles. The moves would take Kroger from having about 8,200 corporate workforce employees to roughly 5,200.“As a company, we have made great progress on many fronts with our customers. We started reducing prices and improving our customer experience in stores and online, and we made investments in simplifying our associates’ lives through technology,” Foran wrote. “Our business is becoming leaner, more focused and more competitive. We are working to be more agile; more precise in our execution; and deliver benefits to our customers, associates and our shareholders.”CEO Foran reportedly said that the changes are intended to reduce duplicative work, lower prices and redirect investment toward store employees as the grocer integrates AI into workflows. Kroger expects to start sharing details about the affected roles in the coming months. The reductions will help the company put more resources toward cutting prices, improving shopping experience and investing in frontline employees, Foran wrote in the memo.Foran, who helped turn around Walmart’s US business in the mid- to late 2010s, is implementing Kroger’s biggest price cuts in years, while making service in stores friendlier and faster. The operator of Fred Meyer and Ralphs chains is also taking a more aggressive approach toward supplier negotiations. The company laid off nearly 1,000 corporate employees last year to cut costs.The three-year downsizing marks the latest decisive shift under Foran's leadership as Kroger works to defend its market share against deep-discount rivals and major big-box retailers.Albertsons wants Kroger to pay $9 billion over failed Kroger dealIncidentally, the layoffs come at the same time when rival grocery chain Albertsons Cos is demanding that Kroger Co pay more than $9 billion for the collapse of the largest US grocery chain merger in history. Albertsons claims Kroger "willfully breached" its contractual commitments and should pay more than $9.3 billion, including a premium stockholders would have gotten and a $600 million termination fee.You use AI every day. articles.title: Antique teddy bear valued at $7,000-$8,000 in 1996 gets a $10,000 updated value in 2026 for its rare white fur and classic features
articles.summary: A white teddy bear named Buffy has received an updated valuation of $10,000, three decades after an antiques expert estimated its auction value at $7,000
articles.body: A white teddy bear named Buffy has received an updated valuation of $10,000, three decades after an antiques expert estimated its auction value at $7,000 to $8,000. The bear appeared on the television programme Antiques Roadshow in Denver in 1996, when toy specialist Noel Barrett examined it and explained the features that made it valuable.According to the PBS Antiques Roadshow, the German-made Steiff bear, believed to date from the mid-1920s, stood out for its 24-inch size, long arms, hump-backed shape and rare white fur. The expert also praised the bear’s excellent condition and careful preservation. The official appraisal now lists its updated auction value at $10,000 in 2026.How did the antique teddy bear’s value change over three decadesWhen Buffy appeared on Antiques Roadshow in 1996, Noel Barrett estimated that the bear could fetch between $7,000 and $8,000 at auction. The owner was astonished and asked whether the expert was kidding. Barrett replied that he was not.Thirty years later, the official appraisal lists Buffy’s updated value at $10,000 at auction. The original valuation was recorded during the programme’s Denver event in 1996. The updated figure gives the bear a higher estimated auction value than it had at the time of its first appraisal. The valuation concerns Buffy, the white Steiff bear featured in the original assessment, rather than her darker companion, Bucky, which the owner said was at home.How did the expert identify Buffy as an antique Steiff bearBarrett dated Buffy to around the mid-1920s. The owner said the bear had been in her possession for about six years before the 1996 appraisal. It had come from her stepfather’s family after her father died and her mother remarried.The owner also had another bear at home named Bucky. He was about the same size as Buffy but had darker fur, and she described him as Buffy’s companion. Barrett recognised Buffy as a German-made Steiff bear by the small button attached to her ear.He explained that Steiff still used buttons in its toys, although their design had changed over the years. Buffy’s button had an early design, with the letter ‘F’ extending beneath it, which helped Barrett estimate the bear’s age.What made Buffy a rare and valuable Steiff teddy bearBarrett pointed to several features that made Buffy a desirable example of a classic teddy bear. Measuring 24 inches, she was a good size for a bear of this type. Her long arms and hump-backed shape were also sought-after features.Her white fur added to her appeal. Barrett explained that white bears, sometimes described as champagne-coloured, were rarer than those with brownish or golden fur.The combination of her size, shape and colour set Buffy apart from more common teddy bears. Barrett also noted the early-style button in her ear, which helped him establish the bear’s age and identify it as a Steiff product.Buffy’s distinctive features made her stand out at appraisalBarrett was impressed by Buffy’s condition, describing her fur as being in very good shape and the bear as exceptional overall. He noted only minor damage, including a small worn patch in the fur. The fabric covering on her feet, however, remained in excellent condition. He added that the shorter fur around her snout was part of the original design, as it had been trimmed during manufacturing.Despite a few minor signs of wear, Buffy was still in excellent condition. Her rare white fur, long arms, hump-backed shape, and 24-inch size also made her stand out. These features, along with the early-style Steiff button in her ear, led Barrett to estimate her auction value at $7,000 to $8,000 in 1996.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Anti-CEC protest in Delhi: Detainees say taken 40km away, beaten
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Many protesters detained Sunday said they were beaten and taken to a community centre in Pandwala Khurd, 38km from Rajiv Chowk, at 8pm and left
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Many protesters detained Sunday said they were beaten and taken to a community centre in Pandwala Khurd, 38km from Rajiv Chowk, at 8pm and left without phones and medical help. They alleged minors were also detained.The claims were confirmed by HC advocate Gaurav Jain, who reached the site. Police denied claims of beatings, and said food, water and first aid were provided. The protesters were released around 9.30pm.How detainees were moved from CP to Chhawla to Pandwala Khurd Nearly 38km from Rajiv Chowk, Delhi High Court advocate Gaurav Jain, found himself at a community centre in Pandwala Khurd, a village he had never heard of, while responding to an SOS by protesters detained Sunday. They alleged minors had been detained alongside other protesters."The location kept changing from Kapashera to Chhawla to ultimately this village I'd never heard of before," he said.Jain reached around 8pm with other lawyers. He alleged he was stopped by cops and was not allowed to meet detainees for several minutes.He said he then called 112 for the police control room van and also contacted the principal magistrate of juvenile justice board-7, asking her to seek a status report from the SHO on the detained minors.Arjun, a detained protester, said in a video message after release, that he was protesting at Connaught Place around 3pm Sunday. He said he saw the cops dragging a couple crossing the road, with no female officers nearby. "The police jumped on us and detained us when we tried to help. They then called women constables," he said.The protesters said they were first taken to an isolated stretch near Rajiv Chowk."We were told to sit in rows... the cops then asked us to hand over our phones and passwords. An inspector... tried accessing one person's photo gallery, saying he was deleting 'aaj ka video'. When the person protested, he was slapped," Arjun alleged.The protesters were then put on another police bus that was divided into 7-8 compartments using iron rods. Arjun alleged that four minors were among them.Despite assurances that cooperation would ensure proper treatment, he alleged, they were beaten up. "There was no space to run as they kept beating us," he said. The bus reached Chhawla police station around 6.53pm.The protesters were taken to the community centre in Pandwala Khurd, where their details, including those of the minors, were recorded.Police, however, said that claims of violence at Pandwala Khurd were baseless and false. It said that no protester was beaten up or assaulted by personnel at the site."Officers had made arrangements to ensure that those detained or present at the location were provided with basic assistance and did not face unnecessary hardship. They came around 8pm and were allowed to leave around 9.30 pm," a senior police officer said.Jain, however, was caught on video pleading with the CRPF personnel guarding the gate: "IO sahab, hume andar aane dijiye. Humare bulane pe hi police aayi hai."The lawyers eventually entered in the PCR van they had called, Jain said. The protesters were released around 9.30pm. One detainee appeared to have injuries on his hand."They had taken away everyone's phone, and when he resisted, he was beaten up. When I asked whether he had received medical assistance, they took him away in a van to help," Jain stated.Police said food and drinking water were provided to the protesters, while those who had sustained injuries were given first aid. Police also denied allegations that anyone's mobile phone had been snatched or that any protester had been subjected to misbehaviour by personnel deployed at Pandwala Khurd."No woman or any other protester was harassed during the operation. Police arrangements continued even after the protesters were released. Buses were provided to facilitate their movement from Pandwala Khurd to the nearest metro stations and bus stands to access public transport and continue their journeys," the officer said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: South Korea’s Kospi index sinks more than 7% on semiconductor share sell-off over AI boom worries
articles.summary: The index was down 7.4% to 5,914.35, its lowest level since late July.
articles.body: HONG KONG — South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index dropped more than 7% Tuesday on a sell-off of chip shares, and Asian shares mostly declined after U.S. stocks ended mixed. U.S. futures were also mixed, and oil prices fell as escalating tensions in the Middle East continued. The Kospi index was down 7.4% to 5,914.35, its lowest level since late July. It reached an all-time high in June after crossing 9,000, supercharged by the global artificial intelligence boom. Samsung Electronics fell 7.7%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 8.8%. Investors’ unease over the AI boom has clouded prospects. Both companies’ stocks fell following reports that the latest advances made by China’s memory chipmaker CXMT could increasingly challenge Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology, the world’s biggest memory chipmakers. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.5% to 67,292.39. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 6.6%. SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1% to 24,033.51. The Shanghai Composite index was 1.1% lower at 3,754.82. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.2% to 8,767.40. Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1.9%, with its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., down 1.6%. On Monday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 edged down 0.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.4%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 0.4%. Chip-related shares traded lower. Nvidia was down 1.3%. Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, was 2.3% lower. Micron Technology lost 3.9%. Broadcom fell 1.9%. Investors are also watching this week’s earnings announcements by major firms including big banks, with Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo reporting results. Oil prices dropped more than 1%. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4% to $105.20 a barrel. That’s still higher than the roughly $72 per barrel in late February, before the Iran war. Benchmark U.S. crude was down 1.5% to $92.34 a barrel. “The market is more concerned over recent developments in the Middle East, with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the lingering risks to oil flows from the Persian Gulf,” wrote ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey in a commentary Tuesday. The U.S. dollar fell to 158.26 Japanese yen from 158.61 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1175, up from $1.1155.

articles.title: How Bollywood and panto merged to create Surinderella show
articles.summary: The production combines bhangra music and classic tale Cinderella to attract new panto audiences.
articles.body:
The creators of the Desi pantomime Surinderella say the show has helped British South Asian audiences see themselves reflected on stage.

The production, described as blending "bhangra beats, colour and magic" with the classic panto tale Cinderella, is touring England and most recently ran in Gravesend, Kent.

Sonya Venugopal, who plays title character Surinder, said the show brought "a whole different diaspora of people" to the traditional genre.

"It feels very groundbreaking and like we're reaching a lot of people that maybe didn't see themselves on stage," she told the BBC.

Artistic director Pravesh Kumar said it was "not very often you get to see British South Asian actors and stories centre stage on English stages".

"This is really rare but our audiences are really mixed, and that's what's really beautiful about it," he said.

"We get to see new British South Asian audiences but also panto audiences are coming and loving it and dancing in the aisles."

The production has two stops in London remaining on its tour: Artsdepot in Barnet on 17 and 18 October and the Theatre Royal Stratford East from 20 to 31 October.

Kumar said Bollywood films had "basically the same story" as Cinderella and were "high drama, high camp, colourful, lots of song and dance".

"The two just married so beautifully together that it just makes complete sense to do it," he said.

Venugopal, who is American, plays the lead role of a young woman stuck doing chores thanks to her self-obsessed stepsisters.

The character's world is turned upside down when she crosses paths with Prince Kavi, with a Bollywood ball and a missing slipper also featuring.

The cast includes former BBC Asian Network presenter Harpz Kaur as Devi Godmother and TV personality Andy Kumar as step-sister Lovely, as well as the costume designer.

He said the design was an "amazing experience to do, just to be able to pull out costumes that sit in both worlds".

Venugopal said the production was "one of the most fun things" she had taken on in her career due to the audience interaction.

"You get to look into the audience, talk to them directly and also see how they're responding," she said. "In other shows that fourth wall is not broken."

articles.title: Melons and aubergines thrive in Oxfordshire hot summer experiment
articles.summary: The exotic fruits were successfully grown this summer at Asthall Manor, near Burford.
articles.body:
Watermelons and aubergines are not crops you might traditionally spot being grown in the UK, but an experiment this summer found them to be performing well in the unusually persistent warm weather.

The exotic fruits were successfully grown at Asthall Manor, near Burford, Oxfordshire, as part of a scheme to boost food resilience in the face of climate change.

The seed experiment coincided with the UK's hottest summer on record - making conditions more appropriate for growing the tropical crops.

Tim Mitchell, who runs the wildlife-friendly kitchen garden at Asthall Manor, said the project aimed to see whether "outdoor-friendly varieties" could now be grown at scale in the UK.

"This year we've had a go at growing watermelons, melons, and aubergines all outdoors - which is not traditionally done in the UK," he explained.

"We weren't even sure it was going to work, but sure enough we had a long hot summer which did allow us to grow these heat-loving crops."

The Crowd Breeding Project is a scheme led by the Gaia Foundation, an international charity which aims to protect and build biodiversity.

Mitchell explained that the scheme was about "building more resilience into our food system in the UK".

"Currently a lot of crops that are grown are very limited in their variety... they're all genetically quite closely related and they're all vulnerable to the same pressures," he said.

"So for instance in a heat drought if they're all very closely genetically related, your entire crop could fail."

As part of the scheme, Mitchell grew different varieties of various tropical crops next to one another.

"Part of the principle that we're working to is to breed genetic diversity into these crops by letting varieties cross through natural cross pollination," he said.

"That means you're growing a diverse flock, and that gives them more genetic breadth to adapt to the changing seasons."

"It's very important that we adapt our crops in this country, not just to increasingly hot summers but potentially to increasingly wet summers. The way you allow crops to adapt is to let them cross with each other and become genetically diverse."

At the moment, Mitchell said many traditional British crops were "not getting the seasons they need" due to changing weather patterns.

"Out of this project, we hope to find new, more resilient, naturally occurring crops," he added.

articles.title: "We had 10 minutes to decide whether to care for our grandchild"
articles.summary: Kinship carers Alan and Julie are full-time guardians to Ella, who has severe disabilities.
articles.body:
Despite a heart attack, giving up his business and having to move house, 65-year-old Alan says taking on the full-time care of his disabled grandchild is the best decision he has ever made.

Nine-year-old Ella, who has severe learning and physical disabilities, has been living with Alan and his wife Julie since she was a baby.

Her parents were unable to care for her and Alan says social services gave the couple just 10 minutes to decide whether to become Ella‘s "kinship carers".

He says: “A social worker said to us, ‘this place closes in about 10 minutes, we need to know if you are prepared to take her on’. ”

More than 140,000 children in England and Wales are being raised by kinship carers like Alan and Julie.

It is the term used for family and friends who take on a child because their parents are unable to care for them.

And according to the charity Kinship's annual survey, seven out of 10 kinship carers say they had “no time to prepare” for the child's arrival.

And four out of 10 report that they had less an hour to decide whether they were able to take a child on.

Unlike foster carers, who are paid by the local authority, kinship carers get no paid leave, no financial assistance and no social workers supporting them.

Alan had just returned from holiday when he was contacted by social services and asked to care for his granddaughter, or she would go into local authority care.

Alan and Julie, who is Ella’s step-grandmother, agreed, but because Ella was a baby and needed 24-hour care, it meant they had to give up their property maintenance business and move from Bradford to Leeds, where Ella lived.

“We would do the same for any of our grandchildren."

Ella was born with Charge Syndrome, a rare genetic disorder, which means she has had to have two heart operations and has learning disabilities.

She attends a special school and is fed through a peg in her stomach.

Julie says: “It was harder because Ella was the only one of our grandchildren who had a disability.

“They told us after we took her on what we would have to do and how we would have to do it.

“It was nerve-wracking and it was hard, but I don’t ever regret taking her and I never will.”

Alan and Julie now have a Special Guardianship Order which means they have parental responsibility until Ella is 18.

Alan has had a heart attack and Julie, who is 66, also has some health problems.

Ella’s aunt Claire recently moved into their council house to help the family manage. She is paid a few hours a week as Ella‘s carer.

Claire says: “She can be cheeky and she is demanding too, but she is just a happy child.

“They (Alan and Julie) have done really well.

“I have seen her as a baby and I have watched her grow up and the change in her is noticeable.”

Lisa Watch, director of policy and communications at Kinship, says: “The outcomes are much better for children to stay within secure, loving families.

“But these families have been under the radar for too long and very often make this life-changing decision overnight and then are not entitled to the support.”

She says the charity helps kinship carers navigate what can be a daunting journey.

Kinship offers free services across the country, including an advice line, peer support groups, free training sessions, workshops and roadshows.

“These children, like any other child that has gone into the care system, will have early trauma and need support and that support just doesn’t automatically exist for these families.”

Ella’s grandparents say they were warned by doctors their granddaughter may never walk - but Ella can now walk unsupported.

Julie says: “She makes us proud every time she does something.”

Alan adds: “Taking Ella on is the best thing I have ever done in my life.

articles.title: Art by modern slavery survivors on display across London
articles.summary: The exhibition organised by Hestia features the work of 26 modern slavery survivors.
articles.body:
"I'm not the person I was six months ago. I'm a person full of possibility."

Victor - not his real name - is a survivor of modern day slavery.

He is describing the impact of creating art in workshops organised by the charity Hestia, which helps people who have been trafficked to rebuild their lives.

He is one of 26 survivors whose work is being featured in the Art is Freedom exhibition that has gone on show across London to raise awareness about the crime.

Victor was born in London. He was trafficked abroad by an organised crime group when he was four and forced into servitude and sexually abused.

He had not drawn since he was five years old, when the abuse began.

"They told me I didn't have any talent and I was useless, and I really believed that.

"Although I was very eager to try to reconnect with art after all these years, I was scared."

Over the past few months, Victor has been taking part in a series of creative workshops along with other survivors.

He said: "It was a place where, even though everybody had suffered trauma in their life, nobody was talking about it.

"We weren't survivors, we were all artists. Nobody felt like a victim in there."

Prior to the workshops, Victor had spent seven years living in isolation, waiting for the Home Office to investigate his case and grant him asylum.

"It was seven years doing absolutely nothing, connecting with no-one, talking to nobody. I was in a very bad place.

"It was like some sort of captivity inside myself, just waiting to die."

He says the workshops have been a "beam of light" in his life helping him rediscover his love of art.

"Now I want to explore more of my talents that have been buried inside me for the past 50 years," added Victor.

If you have been affected by this story the BBC Action Line has a list of organisations which are ready to provide support and advice.

Mary - not her real name - says seeing her work go on display has felt "surreal".

She was imprisoned by her family for the majority of her life, but says art has always felt like an escape.

"I wasn't allowed to interact with people or contact anyone, I was just kept in this room and my purpose to my family was just to help make them money."

Mary's painting is a reflection of how she feels navigating life now she is free.

"It's a faceless mannequin because I felt stripped of my identity and isolated because my experience growing up was so different from other people's."

She says the background represents the beauty she finds in the outside world.

"Since being free I've found so much love for things like flowers, animals and the sky.

"These are things other people take for granted because they're able to see them every day so they've become part of their background noise, but for me it's so vivid how lovely everything is."

Mary says the workshops have felt like a safe and non-judgemental space and an opportunity to connect with other survivors.

"Our experiences are isolating because they're so uniquely traumatic, but we've all experienced something horrifying.

"It's hard to connect with a lot of people you meet outside because you're from a different world to them, but these people were from similar worlds."

Hestia, the charity which organised the workshops and the art show, has said there are up to 130,000 people living in modern slavery in the UK.

CEO, Patrick Ryan, said: "It's a crime which is hidden, it's out of sight. People don't believe it's happening in their neighbourhood, but it is, and it's on the rise."

The UK's independent anti-slavery commissioner Eleanor Lyons helped to curate the exhibition.

She said the cost of living crisis coupled with cuts to support services has created an "increased vulnerability in society", making people more likely to fall into the traps of exploitation.

The low prosecution rate for modern slavery and human trafficking is making it even more attractive to criminals, she added.

"Perpetrators are using new ways to reach and exploit people at scale.

"We know they're using AI, they're hiding behind social media platforms, they're really adapting the way they reach vulnerable victims and they're being ruthless doing so."

articles.title: Roman toddler's drinking cup goes on display in Cirencester museum
articles.summary: The tettine was found in an archaeological dig about 15 years ago but has only just been restored.
articles.body:
A 2nd-Century Roman toddler's cup is being displayed at a museum for the first time.

The cup, or tettine, was found in fragments by archaeologists during excavations in Cirencester, Gloucestershire, in 2011 and has been painstakingly restored.

It will go on display at the town's Corinium Museum with other artefacts found at the same time, and sheds light on a sad story from nearly two millennia ago.

Emma Stuart, museum director, said: "Infant mortality during the Roman period was higher than it is today," adding the tettine had been found with a Roman cockerel figurine thought to have been made to accompany a child's grave, and was likely placed "to provide sustenance to the child's spirit".

Stuart added: "The parents also placed the cockerel, a representative of the god Mercury, to crow the way to the underworld so that the child's spirit didn't get lost on the journey.

"It is a sad and touching story but one that is imbued with care and concern."

The cup was rebuilt and conserved by Lynne Edge, of Edge Conservation, and finished by Wiltshire's Conservation and Museum Advisory Service team, with funding from Friends of Corinium Museum.

"We are proud to have funded the conservation of the tettine cup and to help reunite it with the Corinium Cockerel," said Kathryn Allison from the Friends of Corinium Museum.

The unveiling of the new display coincided with the Cirencester History Festival, which uses the cockerel as its mascot.

"We chose the Corinium Cockerel as our festival logo with great enthusiasm," said Jess Yarrrow, festival director, adding: "It's a nod to the ancient city beneath our feet."

"To see it reunited with the conserved tettine cup after all this time is genuinely special and poignant," she added.

"It connects us directly to the people who walked these streets two millennia ago, which is at the heart of everything our festival stands for."

articles.title: Cost-of-living struggles inspire new supermarket in Newcastle-under-Lyme
articles.summary: New social supermarket offers cheaper groceries with dignity and choice.
articles.body:
"Instead of going to a food bank, being handed a bag and getting back home then finding out that they won't use all those items, at least here they can buy the tokens and shop around for the items they would choose to buy."

Founder Thomas Cliffe hopes the first "social supermarket" in Newcastle-under-Lyme, designed to help people struggling with the cost of living, will offer the "freedom to shop with dignity".

Set up by Community Cupboard NUL CIC, the store allows members to buy groceries at cost price or below, with more choice than other outlets.

Customers can sign up for a membership costing £1 for 12 months. They are then able to purchase tokens to spend on items throughout the store.

Cliffe said the idea was inspired by his own experience after leaving work because of anxiety.

Although his wife was still employed, he said the couple struggled financially and found they were unable to access some forms of support.

"It was horrible because you start to panic and think: 'What am I supposed to do? Where am I going to get the next food from?'"

"We either had to choose a meal or choose the bills."

The supermarket opened for the first time on Monday.

Such stores aim to cut food waste while helping people facing food insecurity by selling surplus goods at lower prices.

"It was exciting to have everyone come through the doors for the first time and give them that freedom to shop with dignity," Cliffe said.

Voluntary co-director Laura Steele said the level of need in the area often went unnoticed.

"One in four children experience poverty from what we have found, and the average income is £29,000."

"There was nothing really for the people of Newcastle and it was crying out for it really," she said.

Cheryl Pepper, a carer who visited after finishing a night shift, described the supermarket as "absolutely brilliant".

"The food's cheap. If you go to Tesco you spend £100, but you come in here, I've put £20 on and I still have some tokens left," she said.

Recent research on the growth of social supermarkets backed the idea that they were less off-putting than food banks and large commercial stores for those facing food insecurity.

But lead researcher, Dr Claire O'Malley from Teesside University, said: "While social supermarkets can improve access to affordable food and reduce waste in the short term, they should not be viewed as a complete solution to food insecurity."

The report called for them to supplement, rather than replace, government support for those struggling to put good food on the table.

Fiona Morris, who has ADHD, said she had often found large supermarkets overwhelming.

After visiting the new store, she said she immediately felt understood by staff.

"It feels like Supermarket Sweep - I feel like I'm robbing the place," she said.

articles.title: Built in 1724, how Jantar Mantar evolved from an astronomical observatory into a symbol of protest in Delhi; now, it is no longer a designated protest site
articles.summary: Delhi’s Jantar Mantar is making headlines again, but this time for a completely different and significant reason.
articles.body: Delhi’s Jantar Mantar is making headlines again, but this time for a completely different and significant reason. Now its role as a public gathering place has ended. On October 12, 2026, reports confirmed that Delhi Police had removed the historic architecture wonder from its list of designated venues for protests and demonstrations. Now Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi have been presented as alternatives. The latest order was issued by Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar on October 11.What Jantar Mantar means for travellersFor travellers exploring Delhi, Jantar Mantar remains one of the must-visit attractions offering a fascinating insight into India's astronomical heritage. The place was built nearly 300 years ago in 1724. It is an unusual complex of geometric structures designed to study the movement of celestial bodies. Over the centuries, it has evolved from an astronomical observatory into a prominent landmark in the heart of modern Delhi.A wonder built in 1724Jantar Mantar was built in 1724 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, the ruler of Amber, near present-day Jaipur. He was a keen student of astronomy and mathematics and wanted to improve astronomical observations in the country. He also wanted to address the limitations of instruments used during his time.He commissioned a series of observatories across northern India, including those in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi. The king commissioned large masonry structures that could be used to observe celestial movements with the naked eye.What can travellers see inside Jantar Mantar?The observatory’s main attractions are open-air scientific instruments, built using brick, rubble and plaster, whose shapes can appear almost abstract at first glance. The complex is home to 13 astronomical instruments.Three of its most prominent structures include:Samrat YantraJai Prakash YantraMisra YantraJourney from an observatory to a protest groundJantar Mantar’s central location is the main reason for its transformation. Its proximity to Connaught Place and the corridors of political power.Over the years, the site witnessed protests by citizens, workers, students and civil society groups seeking attention for their demands. The place gained quite a popularity and became more recognisable during the 2011 anti-corruption movement led by Anna Hazare. During that time, it became the hub for large public gatherings.For many Indians, Delhi’s Jantar Mantar became a symbol of peaceful public protest.Not a protest site anymoreHowever, the latest administrative order marks a change in this role. Following a committee constituted by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs to examine alternative venues for demonstrations, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a designated protest site.Why Jantar Mantar is a must visitFor travellers interested in history, science and architecture, Jantar Mantar offers a different experience from Delhi's forts, tombs and Mughal-era monuments. Its open-air instruments invite visitors to look closely at the relationship between mathematics, the sun, the stars and the passage of time.Its location makes it convenient to combine with a visit to Connaught Place, one of the capital's major commercial and dining districts. Travellers can explore the observatory and then continue to nearby markets, restaurants and other central Delhi landmarks.Jantar Mantar is also a reminder that heritage sites can acquire new meanings as cities change. A place conceived for scientific observation became a landmark of public expression centuries later. Even as its formal status as a designated protest venue changes in 2026, its story continues to reflect the many layers of Delhi's history.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: North Korea’s Kim showcases missile capable of reaching U.S. as Trump signals possible meeting
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a defense industry museum displaying an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States, state media KCNA showed Tuesday.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a defense industry museum displaying an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States, state media KCNA showed Tuesday. The report came a day after President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia. Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in mid-November. Kim, accompanied by his daughter known as Ju Ae and his wife, Ri Sol Ju, attended the opening of the Defense Revolution Museum on Sunday, KCNA said. The museum displayed weaponry developed under Kim’s leadership ranging from drones to the Hwasong-20 intercontinental ballistic missile, KCNA photographs showed. A display in front of the Hwasong-20 launcher appeared to show a multiple warhead design and a world map depicting ranges extending beyond the U.S. mainland to the Middle East, Australia and South America, said Shin Jong-woo, secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum. “The exhibition appears intended to highlight the achievements of Kim’s defense science development program,” Shin said. “It gave the impression of propaganda aimed at gaining a strategic advantage ahead of a potential North Korea-U.S. summit.” Analysts said the museum also reflected a broader effort by Kim to elevate North Korea’s weapons displays into lasting symbols of the regime’s military accomplishments. “By turning what were once temporary weapons exhibitions into a permanent museum, Kim is institutionalizing his military achievements and portraying North Korea’s nuclear and missile buildup as a completed and enduring legacy,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies. Separately, North Korea said it test-fired a tactical ballistic missile on Monday to confirm the successful technical upgrade of an unspecified key component. KCNA said the upgrade marked an important step in improving the performance of all offensive weapons systems, without providing further details. South Korea’s military said Monday that North Korea had fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast. The launch was Pyongyang’s fourth in a month, following Seoul’s recent test of a hypersonic missile.

articles.title: Malaysia’s Firefly cancels flights to Singapore over haze from Indonesia
articles.summary: Move comes as haze from Indonesian fires makes Singapore and Kuala Lumpur the world’s most polluted cities.
articles.body:
Firefly, a Malaysian low-cost airline, has extended the suspension of its flights between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore through Wednesday as smoke from fires in Indonesia continued to blanket the region.

The announcement came as IQAir, an air quality monitor, ranked Singapore and the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur as the world’s two most polluted cities on Tuesday.

Firefly said in a statement that flights between the Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport (SZB) near Kuala Lumpur and the Seletar Airport in Singapore (XSP) have been cancelled up to Wednesday due to “weather and haze conditions”.

It called the action a “proactive safety measure”.

The fires, mostly on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo, are the country’s most intense in 11 years. They have been spurred by El Nino, a weather pattern expected to be among the strongest in four decades.

IQAir, a Swiss air quality monitoring company, said Air Quality Index in Singapore stood at 199 on Tuesday and 183 in Kuala Lumpur. Readings above 150 are generally considered unhealthy, and those above 300 are classified as hazardous.

Firefly, a subsidiary of Malaysia Aviation Group, which includes Malaysia Airlines, first announced the flight cancellations on October 10, citing “low visibility” due to the haze conditions.

Firefly said that affected passengers were being rebooked on Malaysia Airlines flights between Kuala Lumpur International Airport and Singapore’s Changi Airport, subject to seat availability.

The Singapore government has reintroduced subsidised care for haze-related illnesses, as it last did in 2015, when smoke from Indonesian fires hung over the region for weeks.

In Malaysia, schools reopened in most states on Tuesday as air quality improved slightly, but they remain closed in three states, one federal territory and several districts.

Malaysia’s foreign minister, Mohamad Hasan, said on Monday that he would press for stronger regional mechanisms when foreign ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meet next month.

“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he told reporters in Sepang, according to Bernama, Malaysia’s state news agency.

The Philippines, which chairs the bloc this year, confirmed that the issue would be on the agenda.

“It’s in the agenda,” Dominic Xavier Imperial, a spokesman for the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs, said of the November meeting, which will precede the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila.

Mohamad, the Malaysian minister, said Indonesia had deployed about 60,000 personnel to fight the fires, but thick smoke had grounded 34 aircraft, including planes and helicopters.

Remote terrain and limited water supplies have also hindered the effort, he said, and cloud seeding is not possible without suitable rain clouds. He acknowledged Indonesia’s efforts but urged more effective action, citing the toll on Malaysian communities.
